newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax fudge wins government few friends.
newsitem.headline: German tax fudge wins government few friends.

text.p: The German government on Friday avoided the political pitfall of raising petrol taxes but only at the cost of damaging its tax-cutting credentials by putting off a planned cut in an unpopular solidarity surcharge.
The decision goes a long way towards closing a 1997 budget gap that opened this week when the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) blocked parts of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax bill.

But the compromise did little to placate taxpayer groups and drew harsh criticism from commentators, with one newspaper saying Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition had chosen between "plague and cholera".

Waigel said the tax changes would not jeopardise his goal of reducing the budget deficit to 2.5 percent of economic output in 1997, below the three percent required to join the planned start of the single European currency in 1999.
"We will have no higher deficit," Waigel told reporters.

He said the delay in cutting the solidarity surcharge would nearly offset four billion marks ($2.6 billion) lost through an increase in child benefits which went through after the SPD threatened to use its upper house majority to block the tax bill.
A further three billion marks in spending cuts will need to be found in 1997 but Waigel said he would try to spare investment outlays from the austerity pressures.
Parliament's budget committee cleared outstanding questions over tax allowances and inheritance taxes in the remaining rump of the bill. So the measure should now be passed into law.
But SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said the decision not to cut the solidarity surcharge in January 1997 showed the government's tax policy was out of control.
"State finances are so far off course that the government now has to take away tax cuts it promised only yesterday," Lafontaine said.
The conservative Frankfurt Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper said the government had only itself to blame for coming so close to breaking point over its tax bill, part of a major austerity package.
Financial risks had been "recklessly underestimated", it said in an editorial to be published on Saturday.

Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), stood in the way of the petrol tax hike and stressed that they had prevented any tax increases by putting off the cut in the solidarity tax to 6.5 percent from 7.5 percent until 1998.
But that won faint praise from Berlin's Die Welt newspaper, which said: "The truth is that, faced between a choice of plague and cholera, the liberals chose cholera."

In the tradeoff, Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) managed to get the FDP to drop a persistent demand for an early shakeup of Germany's cumbersome tax system -- seen as punishing the honest while offering loopholes which the rich can exploit.
The coalition agreed to introduce major tax reform in 1999, a year later than the FDP wanted and after elections in 1998.
Ahead of the CDU annual party conference next week in Hanover, Kohl's parliamentary lieutenant, Wolfgang Schaeuble, began playing down hopes for major tax cuts in the reform.

He has proposed cutting the top rate of income tax to 35 percent from 53 and lowering the entry rate to 20 percent or below, while scrapping a series of tax breaks. The resultant net cut in taxation would be around 30 billion marks.
But, in an interview with Berlin's Tagesspiegel, Schaeuble said those levels were an ambitious goal, adding that simplifying the tax system was more important than tax cuts.
He also said that a pledge by Kohl not to raise value added tax would only hold until 1998. ($1=1.5423 Mark)
